newsitem.title: DUBAI: Iraq's oil starts to flow again through Gulf.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's oil starts to flow again through Gulf.

text.p: Two huge oil tankers filled with Iraqi crude oil were ready to move through the Gulf in Baghdad's first oil exports through the strategic waterway in six years, Gulf shipping sources said Tuesday.

The resumption of Iraqi sales comes with an added bonus for President Saddam Hussein -- its first customers are American despite the U.S. role as leader of the allied effort that expelled Iraqi invaders from Kuwait in the 1991 Gulf War.

The two cargoes, chartered by Texas-based Coastal Corp. and the energy trading firm Bayoil, were expected to leave Iraq's Mina al-Bakr export terminal in the northern Gulf over the next 24 hours, shipping sources said.

"The Iraqis have been able to load the cargoes quickly ... The (tanker) Star of Africa will depart tonight," one source said, referring to Coastal's chartered vessel, which is expected to take two million barrels of Iraqi crude to the company's refinery on the Caribbean island of Aruba.
Coastal has a contract to take 60,000 barrels per day of crude oil under a United Nations oil-for-food deal that allows Iraq to export up to $2 billion of oil over six months.
Bayoil's 272,000-deadweight-ton Leonidas chartered tanker was expected to complete loading Tuesday and depart on Wednesday as part of what trading sources said was a 30,000 barrel per day contract.
Iraq's first export of oil under the agreement was on Monday, when Turkish refiner TUPRAS took delivery of Iraqi oil at the Mediterranean port of Ceyhan.
At current international oil prices Baghdad is expected to export between 500,000 and 600,000 barrels per day, less than 1 percent of total world supply.
It was exporting 2.7 million barrels daily on the eve of its invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.
